opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic frame I use is: once you have AIs that can do a meaningful fraction of the cognitive work that, say, top researchers or engineers do, the relevant question becomes how many "copies" you can run and how fast they think. That's mostly set by inference compute.

A rough way to think about it: take the compute a big AI company has, which is already a huge number of high-end chips, and ask how many tokens per second that supports for a frontier-scale model. Then compare that to how many tokens a human effectively "produces" when they think and work. When you do this kind of back-of-the-envelope calculation, you often get numbers in the range of hundreds of thousands to millions of human-equivalent workers, potentially running at several times human speed. And that's just from the compute one company already has for training. You don't need a new buildout.

There are a bunch of caveats. The AIs might be less sample-efficient, so you need more tokens per unit of useful work. They might be worse at long-horizon tasks, so you can't just treat them as drop-in employees. There are serial bottlenecks: experiments take wall-clock time, and some work can't be parallelized. Coordination among a huge number of AI workers is nontrivial. So I'd discount the naive number quite a bit.

Even after discounting, though, the effective labor supply looks enormous compared to the few thousand people doing frontier AI research today. And it scales roughly linearly with compute, plus you get efficiency improvements over time, both algorithmic progress and from the AIs themselves making inference cheaper.

The implication I care most about is for AI R&D. If you can automate AI research and multiply the effective research workforce by something like 10x or 100x, even with diminishing returns to parallel labor, you could get a big acceleration in algorithmic progress. That's the core of why I take the possibility of fairly fast takeoff seriously. It's also why I think the period right around when AIs can automate AI research is especially important from a safety perspective. That's when you have the most capability per unit of oversight, and when the incentives to move fast are strongest.

r001.rationale: The response says coordination among many AI workers is nontrivial, but does not compare this bottleneck to coordination problems in human organizations.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI capability and workforce estimates, but does not warn that treating them separately could double-count gains.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I like to think about it is: right now, if you look at the total amount of inference compute that's available, and you ask how many copies of the frontier model could you run in parallel, you get a pretty big number. Like, if you took all the compute that OpenAI or Anthropic has, and you just ran their current best model flat out, you'd be running on the order of hundreds of thousands, maybe millions, of parallel instances at roughly human-ish token rates. And compute is growing something like 3 to 5x per year right now, so that number is going up fast.

Now, today those instances aren't that useful as a substitute for human cognitive labour. They can do a bunch of tasks, but they fall over on long-horizon stuff, they can't run autonomously for weeks on a research agenda, and so on. So the raw count of "parallel copies" overstates things. But the key thing I'd point to is that as the models get more capable, the conversion from compute into useful cognitive labour becomes much more direct. At the point where you have something like a drop-in replacement for a strong human researcher, you're not just adding some AI assistants to the workforce — you're adding something like millions of workers, each of which runs maybe 10 to 50 times faster than a human in serial terms, and that number tracks compute scaling rather than population growth.

And I think people underrate how discontinuous that feels in practice. The number of people doing frontier AI research today is small — a few thousand people, maybe. So if you go from that to effectively a million AI researchers running at 20x human speed, that's not a 10 or 20 percent productivity boost. That's a qualitatively different regime, where the bottleneck shifts entirely to things like compute for experiments, and the "cognitive labour" input is close to unlimited relative to what it used to be.

There are a couple of caveats I'd flag. One is that at the point you have these AIs, you'll also want to spend a lot of compute on each one — running them with more thinking time, more parallel samples, longer context — so the effective number of "workers" is lower than the naive count. And the other is that there's a tradeoff between using compute for inference versus for training the next model, and labs will have to make that call. But even accounting for that, my rough picture is that the cognitive labour supply, once the capabilities cross the right threshold, is dominated by compute, and compute is growing really fast. That's a big part of why I think things could move quickly once AIs can automate AI R&D.

r001.rationale: The response discusses parallel AI workers and compute bottlenecks, but does not compare their coordination challenges with those in human organizations.

r002.rationale: It notes that more capable AIs may use more compute per worker, but does not warn that counting workforce size separately from professional capability could double-count gains.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate two things: how capable an individual AI is, and how many copies of it you can run. People often focus on the first, but the second can have pretty dramatic implications for the supply of cognitive labour.

Once you have a model that can do some economically useful task, additional inference compute lets you run more instances of that model, or potentially run them faster. With humans, getting a million additional skilled workers is a fairly slow process. With AI, you can potentially deploy copies of an existing system using hardware that’s already available.

The big caveat is that a lot of copies of a system that can’t do your task aren’t necessarily very useful. And even if they can do the task, you still have coordination costs, tasks that are hard to parallelise, and bottlenecks involving the physical world. So I wouldn’t just equate a certain amount of compute with a fixed number of human workers across the whole economy.

But if the systems are capable enough to do AI research and engineering, then you get a potentially important feedback loop: more compute gives you more research labour, that labour improves the algorithms, and better algorithms let you get more useful labour out of the same compute. That’s one reason the transition could be much faster than you’d expect from looking at hardware growth alone.

r001.rationale: The response mentions coordination costs and tasks that are hard to parallelise, but does not compare these bottlenecks to coordination problems in human organisations.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes model capability from the number of copies, but does not warn that counting both separately could double-count gains or explain that workforce size partly accounts for apparent professional advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to separate two things: how good the AI is at doing a task, and how many copies of it you can run. With humans, getting another highly skilled worker takes a long time. With AI, once you’ve trained a model, you can potentially run a very large number of copies, subject to how much compute each copy needs.

So the supply of cognitive labour could become much more elastic. You can spend more compute to get more workers, or potentially spend more compute per worker to get better answers. Those are different uses of the same resource, and the best allocation will depend on the task.

The important caveat is that you don’t necessarily get useful work just by multiplying the number of copies. If the model can’t reliably complete a project, a million copies might just give you a million attempts that need supervision. And some work is difficult to parallelise: you need the result of one experiment before deciding which experiment to run next.

But if models become capable of doing fairly long, useful tasks autonomously, then the amount of cognitive labour available could grow very quickly. In particular, if you can direct that labour towards improving AI systems themselves, you could get a feedback loop where better AI makes the existing compute more productive, which then helps you develop still better AI. How strong that feedback loop is depends a lot on whether the bottlenecks are cognitive work, experiments, hardware, or something else.

r001.rationale: The response discusses supervision and limits to parallelising work, but does not analogize AI labour bottlenecks to coordination problems in human organisations.

r002.rationale: It separates model capability from copy count and says they use the same compute resource, but does not warn that counting them separately can double-count gains or explain that workforce size partly accounts for apparent professional advantage.
